Poster number & title: 1 - Automation and AI-Driven Morphological Profiling of Organoids for Drug Discovery
Abstract: Three-dimensional organoid models of breast and lung cancer now enable more physiologically relevant drug assessment, particularly for agents targeting DNA-damaging and apoptotic mechanisms. However, robust phenotypic profiling of these organoids requires methods that are quantitative, highly reproducible, and scalable. Leveraging the label-free, non-invasive capabilities of brightfield imaging, we established an automated, high-throughput workflow  utilizing the Operetta CLS high-content imaging system and Arivis AI- driven analysis software.  High-content imaging provides rapid, standardized acquisition of high-resolution brightfield datasets across extensive organoid cohorts, eliminating staining artifacts and batch variability. Automated image processing with Arivis employs deep neural networks for precise organoid segmentation, detailed morphometric feature extraction, and identification of drug-induced morphological changes —including nuclear fragmentation, condensation, and growth arrest —across a wide range of experimental conditions. This integrated system supports label-free, multiparametric phenotyping at scale, delivering objective and consistent quantification essential for differentiating responses for DNA-damaging and apoptotic drugs of interests.  By enabling high-throughput image capture and unbiased AI- powered analysis, this platform markedly accelerates drug screening  while minimizing subjective operator influence and manual workload. Our automated workflow facilitates discovery and prioritization of candidate therapeutics for breast and lung cancers, and is readily adaptable to diverse organoid models and drug mechanisms. Continued development will expand its application to additional imaging modalities and disease contexts, supporting the next generation of preclinical phenotypic drug discovery.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 2 - Unsupervised Phenotype Discovery in High-Content Imaging via Archetypes and Self-Supervised Learning
Abstract: Identifying novel therapeutic candidates for complex diseases remains a major challenge in modern drug discovery. To address this, biopharmaceutical research increasingly relies on automated, high-throughput screening assays using cell culture models to evaluate thousands of compounds in parallel. However, the resulting large-scale imaging data complicates systematic expert review, making phenotype discovery and classification dependent on extensive—and often biased—manual curation. A common strategy to mitigate this issue is archetypal analysis, which identifies phenotypes within a dataset. In this work, we introduce an end-to-end deep learning framework that simultaneously learns embeddings from high-content images and uncovers phenotypic structures without supervision [1]. Building on these representations, we apply self-supervised learning to construct a phenotypic embedding space, enabling intuitive visual exploration and downstream assay analysis. Comprehensive experiments on industry-relevant assays demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing unsupervised and supervised methods, providing a scalable and unbiased pipeline for drug screening and functional genomics [2]. Poster number & title: 3 - Agentic AI Enables Automated CellProfiler Pipeline Design via Multimodal In-Context Learning
Abstract: Designing image analysis pipelines in CellProfiler typically demands expert knowledge and extensive manual tuning, creating barriers to scalability and accessibility in high-throughput biological research. In this proof-of-concept study, we introduce an agentic workflow that harnesses in-context learning and multimodal AI models to automatically generate CellProfiler pipelines from minimal user input. Our approach enables a vision-language model to function as an autonomous agent: interpreting example images and textual prompts, reasoning over visual features, and producing complete  pipeline configurations tailored to new datasets. Leveraging a few- shot learning paradigm, the system generalizes from a single  annotated example—comprising an image, text, and documentation context—to generate parameterized pipelines for tasks such as segmentation and object detection, adapted to the biological context presented. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that the AI-generated pipelines achieve performance comparable to expert-designed configurations while reducing complexity. These findings highlight the potential of agentic AI to streamline and democratize biomedical image analysis by minimizing domain-specific expertise requirements and simplifying pipeline design.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 4 - Enabling Ultra-High Throughput Cell Painting for Drug Discovery
Abstract: Morphological screening is a powerful tool with the potential to narrow down mechanisms of actions in an unbiased manner, predict the toxicity of compounds, and contribute to the development of more first-in-class medicines, thereby offering potential for an improved understanding of diseases. The Cell Painting assay (CPA) is an image-based procedure that utilizes several dyes to stain various cellular components and allows for the extraction of hundreds to thousands of morphological features that are used to construct phenotypic profiles of treatment conditions. However, achieving significant throughput with the CPA is often met with challenges including image acquisition speed and scalability in a high throughput format. Here, we optimized the CPA for the Araceli Endeavor®- a high speed and high content imaging platform that generates high resolution images fit for morphological profiling. Our modified CPA utilized of a panel of five cellular stains captured in the four separate fluorescent channels of the Endeavor®. With the Endeavor® platform, we consistently capture high-quality staining of U-2 OS cells in both CellVis 384-well and Greiner 1536-well plates in under 10 minutes. We also demonstrate our ability to characterize distinct morphological profiles from a panel of reference chemicals used in Willis, et al. 2020 in both 384 and 1536 plate densities. Ultimately, we demonstrate the success of performing our modified CPA in both 384- and 1536-well plates and utilizing the high-content images from the Endeavor® to construct morphological profiles of various compounds with known mechanisms of action.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 5 - In Silico Labeling Enables Accurate Phenotypic Profiling for Hit Discovery and Hit Expansion
Abstract: In silico labeling (ISL) is a computational microscopy technique leveraging GenAI to predict fluorescent staining from brightfield (BF) images. By virtually multiplexing multiple fluorescent readouts, ISL  offers substantial cost-savings that expand capabilities for high- content imaging. However, critical questions regarding ISL’s  accuracy in phenotypic profiling remain underexplored. This study systematically evaluates ISL’s performance across 50,000 diverse compounds in key drug discovery scenarios. First, we investigated ISL’s accuracy in predicting phenotype modulation across varied perturbagens. This included training on ~400 compounds with known mechanism of action from 10 fluorescence probes, and validation on 50,000 diverse compounds. ISL reliably predicted 10 imaging channels from BF inputs, showing over 80% overlap with ground-truth staining in unsupervised hit  identification. Virtual multiplexing by ISL also revealed novel probe- specific hits, capturing subtle phenotypes beyond stained channels.  Second, we evaluated ISL’s ability to predict bioactivity by retrospectively benchmarking ISL-generated profiles for hit expansion against 270 historical primary assays. Orthogonal imaging fingerprints derived from ISL achieved a 4-fold average increase in hit rate enrichment for cell-based assays and a 2-fold increase for cell-free assays. ISL also demonstrated complementarity to Morgan fingerprints, robust correlation with staining-based methods, that enhanced hit diversity through multiplexed imaging fingerprints. This study showcases ISL as a powerful tool for phenotypic profiling and drug discovery, with scalable accuracy and enriched bioactivity predictions across distinct assay modalities. As ISL continues to mature, it has the potential to become a cornerstone of modern drug discovery to enable efficient biological fingerprinting for hit identification and expansion.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 6 - A Multiplex Cellular Model of Niemann-Pick Type C Genetic Disease for Live-Cell  High Conntent Imaging
Abstract: Rare genetic diseases present unique challenges due to limited access to patient cells and a lack of cellular and animal models. Niemann–Pick type C (NPC) disease is a rare and fatal neurodegenerative disorder (1:150,000) caused by mutations in the gene encoding the NPC1 protein responsible for intracellular lipid trafficking. These mutations lead to large lysosomal accumulation of unesterified cholesterol and cellular damage that can be detected by high-content imaging technologies. We recently developed a single plasmid technology for CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing that facilitates the generation of cellular models of human diseases. The system allows multiplex insertion of labeling tags into endogenous genes for protein detection and the insertion of targeted mutations at specific genomic regions. This enables the development of cellular models for high-content imaging drug discovery in live cells without the use of chemical staining or immunofluorescence. In this study, we created a cellular model of NPC disease using HeLa cells by employing the one plasmid system for genome editing. We introduced the most common mutation of NPC1 and tagged three endogenous proteins with fluorescent markers to detect subcellular structures in live cells. We confirmed large phenotypic differences in the number, size, and signal intensity of lysosomes in NPC1 mutated cells. We used the novel NPC cellular model to screen a library of autophagy modulators and identified compounds that reduce lysosomal enlargement and accumulation. In conclusion, this model accurately recapitulates the lysosomal accumulation phenotype observed in NPC patients and can be used for high-content imaging-based drug discovery.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 7 - Automated cell-based assays for drug discovery and enhanced biomanufacturing pipelines using AI
Abstract: Modern biomedical research increasingly relies on automation, with robust image-based assays driving rapid discovery. AI-driven assays can enhance both biopharma discovery and manufacturing.  In drug discovery, phenotypic profiling is essential for effectively identifying subtle effects in high-content drug screens. Existing imaging and analysis technologies are being challenged by the increased use of 3D cultures to benefit from their significant richness and corresponding complexity. ViQi’s AI-based toolkit AutoHCSTM has been used both for high-content assay optimization and treatment effect detection: when presented with bioprinted 3D brain cancer cultures treated with test compounds, it reliably distinguished candidate anti-cancer compounds across multiple doses that differ in mechanism. While phenotypic separation between compounds improved with increasing z-planes, it did not scale linearly with increasing z-planes. This finding enables assay workflow improvements optimized for image acquisition time, computing, and storage costs.  At the stage of biomanufacturing in biopharma, optimization relies on automated assays to monitor the process . Cells are ideal reporters for key variables that characterize the biomanufacturing workflow. ViQi’s Automated Viral Infectivity Assay (AVIA™) uses machine learning and brightfield microscopy to detect viral infection in live cells, outputting a quantitative infectivity measure without the need for sample preparation or fluorescent markers. Alternatively, AVIA can also be used for viral clearance through extended incubations, which can increase sensitivity to the limiting dilution range. Both assays use high-throughput, image-based analysis, with AI interpreting complex visual data faster,more precisely and more generally than conventional methods.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 8 - Transparent, autonomous, agentic AI for mechanistic analysis of high-content phenotypic data
Abstract: The exponential increase in biomedical data, including multi-omics and high-content phenotypic data, offers unprecedented opportunities for understanding biological mechanisms and accelerating drug discovery, yet the sheer amount of data overwhelms traditional analysis methods. Here we introduce a framework for autonomous artificial intelligence (AI)-driven drug discovery that integrates knowledge graphs with large language models (LLMs). This system is capable of planning and carrying out automated data mining and data analysis programs to make novel discoveries, develop new hypotheses, and iteratively test those hypotheses using vast quantities of public or private data. Throughout this process, the system provides transparent details of its research strategies, progress, and supporting data, enabling a thorough assessment of its methods and findings by human researchers.  At the heart of this framework lies the “focal graph” - a novel construct that harnesses centrality algorithms to distill vast, noisy datasets into concise, data-driven hypotheses. By enabling high-throughput search and automated result interpretation, such a framework could be used to execute massive numbers of searches to identify patterns across complex, diverse datasets and prioritize actionable hypotheses at a scale and speed unachievable by human researchers alone.  We present an autonomous, agentic focal-graph based platform that can analyze cell painting and multi-omics data, yielding novel insights relevant to multiple stages of biomedical research and drug discovery.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 9 - Dual morphological profiling approaches to characterize schizophrenia in an in vitro placental model
Abstract: Trophoblast stem cells (TSCs) represent a powerful tool for the in vitro study of placental development and function. As placental health has been shown to be critical in brain development and potential risk for schizophrenia (SCZ), we leveraged Cell Painting to profile 23 genotypically distinct TSC lines derived from human patient iPSCs from SCZ (13 lines) and non-SCZ donors (10 lines). Imaging data was used to generate both traditional (CellProfiler) and CNN-derived feature profiles. Profiles were used to train Random Forest classifiers of sex and diagnosis (Dx), two attributes likely driving line-to-line morphological differences. Sex classifiers showed strong performance as measured by ROC AUC with 10-fold cross validation (median AUC>0.87). Mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum granularity showed significant decreases in male lines as compared to females, indicating highly salient sexual dimorphism in TSCs. Dx classifiers also showed good performance (median AUC~0.8). Interestingly, nuclear features, including several related to texture and shape (e.g., solidity), comprised many of the top features driving Dx classification. Finally, we examined the effect of hypoxia, a placental stressor, on sex and Dx classifiers and observed significant changes in feature importance: notably, nuclear area/shape features were no longer among the most important for Dx classification, suggesting that hypoxia may induce cellular changes that obfuscate certain morphological differences between SCZ and control cells.  Collectively, these findings indicate that image-based profiling using Cell Painting can identify subtle morphological changes in a genetically diverse set of TSC lines derived from patients with SCZ, along with changes induced by physiologically significant disturbances.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 10 - AI-Driven Target Deconvolution Identifies α-Terthienyl as a Dual DPP-IV/HSD17B13 Modulator
Abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is the most common chronic liver disease worldwide and lacks broadly effective therapies. To address this need, we developed a Cell Painting–style high-content phenotypic screening assay using PH5CH8 human hepatocytes to identify small molecules that modulate induced hepatic steatosis. Cells were lipid-loaded with sodium oleate, stained with multiplexed fluorescent probes, and imaged on the Yokogawa CV8000 platform. Segmentation (CellPose/CellProfiler) and feature extraction (>500 features per cell) were combined with machine learning (XGBoost) for robust identification of steatosis-modulating compounds. Screening of a 5,300-compound annotated bioactive library identified 15 inhibitors and 16 exacerbators of steatosis. The Plex AI platform was then applied for target enrichment analysis, which revealed mechanistic convergence across hits and uncovered a novel bidirectional role for Wnt/β-catenin signaling. For the most potent and non-toxic inhibitor, α-terthienyl (EC₅₀ ~120 nM), Plex predicted DPP-IV and HSD17B13 as putative targets. Biochemical assays confirmed α-terthienyl as a direct DPP-IV inhibitor, while an oxidized metabolite inhibited HSD17B13. Molecular docking supported these interactions, suggesting a dual-target polypharmacology that integrates systemic glucose regulation with liver-specific lipid metabolism. In diet-induced obese mice, α-terthienyl significantly reduced hepatic steatosis, improved glucose tolerance, and lowered serum ALT/AST in 12-days when administered via daily IP injection at 5mg/kg. This study demonstrates the value of integrating high-content imaging, machine learning, and AI-driven enrichment/target deconvolution to accelerate therapeutic discovery. α-Terthienyl emerges as a promising MASLD lead, illustrating a workflow that connects unbiased phenotypic screening to mechanistic insight for drug discovery.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 11 - Using multiplex fluorescent staining to identify a specific CDK2 inhibition state
Abstract: The current standard of care for hormonal-sensitive metastatic breast cancer is a combination of CDK4/6 inhibitor (CDK4/6i) with endocrine therapy (ET). These agents suppress tumour progression by inhibiting CDK-mediated phosphorylation of retinoblastoma (RB), resulting in RB-dependent cell cycle arrest. However, CDK4/6i + ET resistance is common in the clinic; thus, a novel therapeutic agent is needed. Recent studies have shown that the CyclinE-CDK2 axis, which regulates late G1/S cell cycle progression, is one of the most common mechanisms of resistance for CDK4/6i + ET therapy. However, the role of CDK2 in the cell cycle is more complex than that of CDK4/6. CDK4/6 is viewed as a strictly G1/S cell cycle regulator, and its function can be assessed by measuring the phosphorylation status of RB (S807/811). On the other hand, CDK2 phosphorylates a wide range of substrates across multiple cell cycle checkpoints. CDK2 also plays a critical role in regulating DNA replication during mitosis. To date, there is no specific measurement of CDK2 activity. Most preclinical studies rely on non-CDK2-specific assays, such as EdU pulse labeling and RB phosphorylation status. In this work, we utilize the Iterative Indirect Immunofluorescence Imaging (4i) technique to measure up to twelve cell cycle markers across eight cell lines with various degrees of Cyclin E/CDK2 dependency. The 4i technique allows large-scale staining with relatively minimal cost. This work aims to identify a set of markers that can distinguish a specific CDK2-inhibited state, leading to better lead optimization and improved patient selection for CDK2 inhibition treatment.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 12 - Revitalizing Structural Similarity for Bright-field to Fluorescence Microscopy Image Translation
Abstract: Virtually translating bright-field images to fluorescence images can enhance efficiency and avoid dye toxicity. However, prior pixel-wise and conventional perceptual loss functions often fail to capture fine structural and contrast details, resulting in blurred outputs. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel Multi-Scale Contrast-Structure Consistency Loss (MS-CSL) that revitalizes the traditional SSIM loss by focusing solely on the contrast and structure components while discarding the luminance component. This design is motivated by our observation that contrast and structure play a crucial role in downstream tasks, whereas luminance has minimal impact. MS-CSL employs a Gaussian pyramid to enforce multi-scale contrast-structure consistency, with spatial pooling as an attention mechanism to highlight key regions. Combined with a Laplacian pyramid-based multi-scale input and a UNet architecture, our model effectively generates high-fidelity fluorescence images. Experiments demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing methods in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 13 - Improved Brightfield Segmentation of Organoids in Image Artist and Harmony Image Analysis Software
Abstract: Monitoring organoid cultures using brightfield microscopy is essential, providing valuable information such as size, morphology and evolution of structures throughout the culture. In pharmacological research, variations in size are commonly used to assess the response of organoids to different treatments, providing indications of the efficacy or toxicity of the molecules tested. As the use of fluorescent markers is limited in the long term for live cell imaging, temporal monitoring relies mainly on brightfield microscopy. However, automated analysis of brightfield images remains more complex than fluorescence: brightfield images feature low contrast, complex backgrounds and lack specific labeling, making precise detection of objects of interest difficult. Additionally, many organoid types are grown in Matrigel domes at different depths, resulting in apparent superposition in brightfield projection images. This study introduces an enhanced image segmentation approach for organoid detection in dome cultures using Image Artist and Harmony image analysis software. Our improved methodology addresses key challenges including varying z-heights requiring z-stack imaging, significant size and morphological variations between patient-derived organoids, overlapping structures in dense cultures, morphological changes during maturation, and artifacts from well rims. By implementing a new 2.5D analysis approach that calculates variance images, detects domes as regions of interest, creates minimum intensity projections, and finally detects different types of organoids, we achieved approximately twice the detection rate compared to previous methods. This improved segmentation method provides more accurate organoid quantification for research and quality control applications in organoid-based studies.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 14 - Decoding Cellular Phenotypes with PhenoVue Live and Endpoint Cell Painting Kits
Abstract: High-content imaging (HCI) combined with Cell Painting provides a powerful approach for multiplexed phenotypic profiling, enabling the detection of subtle cellular responses to drugs and mechanisms of action. Revvity’s PhenoVue Cell Painting Kits, available in endpoint, live-cell, and multi-organelle formats, offer ready-to-use reagents optimized for reproducibility and biological relevance. Configurable options allow antibody integration to expand biological specificity. Comparative studies show that live Cell Painting improves sensitivity for dynamic phenotypes and kinetic analyses, while multi-organelle assays enhance separation of specific compound classes. Both formats complement standard Cell Painting, providing broader insights into phenotypic diversity. Across all applications, the kits demonstrate minimal impact on cell health, making them suitable for both short- and long-term assays. Together, these tools extend the resolution of phenotypic screening and support drug discovery workflows from early screening to mechanistic characterization.

Poster number & title: 15 - Quantifying Antibody and ADC Internalization and Lysosomal Trafficking by High-Content Imaging
Abstract: Antibody internalization and subsequent trafficking to lysosomes are critical processes for antibody–drug conjugate (ADC) efficacy, directly influencing payload delivery and receptor regulation. Traditional methods to assess internalization often require multiple wash steps and provide limited temporal or spatial resolution. Here, we introduce the PhenoVue™ Human Antibody Internalization Kit, a no-wash, pH-sensitive assay optimized for live-cell high-content imaging (HCI). The assay employs a fluorophore that remains quenched at neutral extracellular pH but fluoresces upon entry into acidic endo-lysosomal compartments, thereby selectively reporting bona fide internalization and lysosomal trafficking events. Using A431 (EGFR+), SKOV3, and BT-474 (HER2+) cells treated with cetuximab or trastuzumab, in both naked antibody and ADC formats, we quantified uptake and trafficking through kinetic and dose-response experiments. Results revealed rapid EGFR-mediated internalization in A431, contrasted with slower HER2 uptake in SKOV3 and BT-474, consistent with established receptor biology. Confocal imaging confirmed trafficking of antibody targeted receptor to lysosomal compartments. The kit is compatible with 96- and 384-well plate formats, enabling throughput flexibility, and integrates seamlessly with high-performance HCS systems such as Opera Phenix™ Plus and Operetta CLS™. Combined with Harmony software for straightforward image analysis and data manipulation, this workflow supports efficient, standardized internalization studies. Together, these findings demonstrate that the PhenoVue Human Antibody Internalization Kit provides a robust, scalable, and biologically relevant platform to study internalization and endo-lysosomal trafficking of both naked and ADC antibodies, supporting basic research and therapeutic development pipelines.

Poster number & title: 16 - SynapSeg: A Pipeline for Quantifying Small, Sparse Structures in 3D Microscopy
Abstract: Accurate segmentation of small, sparse structures in 3D microscopy remains challenging, especially where generating high quality ground truth data is labor-intensive. Here, we develop SynapSeg, an open-source pipeline for cochlear ribbon synapse analysis, serving as a case study for high-accuracy image analysis of small, sparse biological structures. This approach includes (1) interactive tools for rapid semi-automatic ground truth generation, (2) a custom 3D U-net trained on a multi-lab dataset from multiple microscope modalities, and (3) modular prediction-to-analysis workflows, including synapse pair analysis and morphological metrics. Implemented as both a command-line tool and a Napari plugin, SynapSeg facilitates human-in-the-loop annotation and model refinement and scalable, reproducible analysis. By training on a range of data from varying microscopes and with varying resolution, these tools are designed to work across diverse datasets. While developed for auditory neuroscience, this framework offers  a generalizable strategy for segmentation and morphological quantification of sparse subcellular structures in other biological domains. Ongoing and future work aims to integrate these tools with multi-modal datasets of synaptic imaging and functional auditory neuronal electrophysiology measurements to link synaptic structure and function.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 17 - Whole slide chemical imaging within clinical timeframes using QCL microscopy
Abstract: Infrared (IR) spectroscopic microscopy enables label-free biomedical imaging with broad molecular sensitivity. One of the major limitations for clinical applications of IR spectroscopic imaging modalities is the acquisition time required to obtain reasonable images of tissues with high spatial resolution and good signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Using a traditional Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) microscope, the time to acquire a reasonable signal to noise spectroscopic scan of a standard microscope slide region of tissue can take many hours. Empowered by quantum cascade lasers (QCL), recent instrumentation developments now allow for label-free chemical imaging of entire microscope slides in under 30 minutes, enabling rapid, high quality spectroscopic imaging of tissues within clinical timeframes. Here we compare the data from a novel QCL microscope to an FTIR microscope covering multiple aspects of spectroscopic imaging of a large, clinically relevant, prostate cancer tissue cohort (N = 1281). Comparisons of hyperspectral data acquisition quality in both achieved signal to noise and image contrast alongside the capacity for unsupervised and supervised modelling of tissue constituents are reported. We conclude that it is now possible to collect comprehensive molecular information intrinsically from tissue sections and derive clinically relevant data in a timeframe suitable for translation into the pathology laboratory.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 18 - Pancancer network analysis reveals key master regulators for cancer invasiveness
Abstract: Tumor invasiveness reflects numerous biological changes, including tumorigenesis, progression, and metastasis. To decipher the role of transcriptional regulators (TR) involved in tumor invasiveness, we performed a systematic network-based pan-cancer assessment of master regulators of cancer invasiveness. We stratified patients in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) into invasiveness high (INV-H) and low (INV-L) groups using consensus clustering based on an established robust 24-gene signature to determine the prognostic association of invasiveness with overall  survival (OS) across 32 different cancers. We devise a network- based protocol to identify TRs as master regulators (MRs) unique to  INV-H and INV-L phenotypes. We validated the activity of MRs coherently associated with INV-H phenotype and worse OS across cancers in TCGA on a series of additional datasets in the Prediction of Clinical Outcomes from the Genomic Profiles (PRECOG) repository. Using 24-gene signature, we defined the invasiveness score for each patient sample and stratified patients into INV-H and INV-L clusters. We observed that invasiveness was associated with worse survival outcomes in almost all cancers and had a significant association with OS in ten out of 32 cancers. Our network-based framework identified common invasiveness-associated MRs specific to INV-H and INV-L groups across the ten prognostic cancers, including COL1A1, which is also part of the 24-gene signature, thus acting as a positive control. Downstream pathway analysis of MRs specific to INV-H phenotype resulted in the identification of several enriched pathways,  including EMT pathway, TGF-β signaling pathway, regulation of Toll- like receptors, cytokines, and inflammatory response, selective expression of chemokine receptors.

Poster number & title: 19 - AI-Powered Label-Free Cell Quantification via Transmitted Light Imaging
Abstract: Label-free imaging offers significant advantages over traditional fluorescence-based methods, including reduced reagent costs, faster processing, and the ability to monitor live cells without introducing labeling artifacts. In this study, we used customizable AI models  within IN Carta Image Analysis Software to develop deep learning- based segmentation models for accurate cell and nuclear detection  using transmitted light (TL) images alone. We began by establishing label-free analysis using the U2OS cell line. To develop a TL-based nuclear segmentation model, we first applied a pre-trained AI model to segment nuclei in Hoechst-stained images. The resulting segmentation masks, paired with corresponding TL images, were used to train a new model capable of segmenting nuclei using TL images only. This approach enabled label-free nuclear detection with around 97% accuracy, as validated against Hoechst-based nuclear counts. We further trained the model using images from additional cell lines, including HeLa, HCT116, U2OS, MCF7, and HEK. The model achieved over 90% accuracy across most of these cell types. To evaluate its utility in compound screening, we treated the five cell lines with 10 anti-cancer compounds using a 7-point dilution series. Cell counts obtained via TL-based nuclear segmentation were compared to traditional nuclear staining methods across treatments. The results showed strong correlation and comparable IC50 values, confirming the accuracy and reliability of the label-free approach. Overall, this label-free approach offers significant advantages in processing speed and workflow simplicity, enabling real-time  analysis of compound effects and making it a powerful tool for high- throughput and phenotypic screening applications.
Category: Advancements in Image-Based AI & Foundation Models for Drug Discovery

Poster number & title: 20 - Single-Molecule Resolution Spatial Transcriptomics Enabled by HCS.ai
Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics is needed to understand how genes are expressed within their specific locations in a tissue. Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics, however, faces challenges in accurate transcript assignment to cells, signal intensity limitations, and scaling up experiments. Accurate cell segmentation is crucial for assigning transcripts to their correct cellular origin. Existing cell segmentation methods can be inaccurate, leading to over- or under segmentation, misassigning transcripts, and requiring manual intervention. Here we used the next-generation high-content imager, ImageXpress HCS.ai System, and the AI-enabled image analysis software, IN Carta Image Analysis Software. The HCS.ai system renders fast, high-throughput acquisition and improved overall sensitivity, enabling the detection of dim or low-signal single molecules, and IN Carta software was equipped with AI-based object segmentation and classification modules, allowing fast and accurate cell segmentations. Hela cells were seeded in a 384 well plate and the IL-6 expression were induced with TNF-α and IL-1β, followed by the fixation and hybridization of SDHA- and IL6-specific target probes. The RNA  signals were amplified with a successive hybridization of pre- amplifier probes, amplifier probes and label probes (ViewRNA Cell  Plus Assay, ThermoFisher) and imaged on the HCS.ai system. After analysis in IN Carta software, we found on average over 6-fold increase in IL6 expression in IL6-stimulated Hela cells compared to non-stimulated Hela cells. Overall, the ImageXpress HCS.ai System together with IN Carta Image Analysis Software offer a systematic solution for detecting single molecules by facilitating precise cell segmentation and enhancing low signal detection, enabling accurate transcript detection and assignment to cells.

Poster number & title: 21 - Coupling image-based functional profiling and proteomics to investigate mitochondrial dysfunction
Abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a central pathological feature in metabolic diseases, cardiovascular diseases, and neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s disease.Furthermore, identifying mitochondrial toxicity early in the drug development pipeline allows for prioritisation of candidates likely for success. To understand the multifaceted consequences of mitochondrial dysfunction, we developed a novel platform for multidimensional functional phenotyping, dubbed “MitoPaint”. This assay simultaneously labels mitophagy, mitochondria membrane potential (MMP) and reactive oxygen species (ROS). Microscopy images are then analysed to generate a multiparametric phenotypic profile of several thousand features describing the morphology, texture and intensity of mitochondrial functional fluorophores within the cell. In SH-SY5Y, “MitoPaint” robustly captured drug-induced mitochondrial phenotypes, which cluster in a dose-dependent and mechanism of action (MOA) dependent manner. In a simulated drugs creen of 38 drugs and mitochondrial toxicants, shared nearest-neighbour clustering grouped like-for-like “MitoPaint” profiles, identifying similarity between drugs of similar MOA. Armed with this evidence from “MitoPaint” profiling, it was explored whether the molecular mechanisms underpinning these phenotypic profiles could be rationalised at the protein level. Data-independent acquisition(DIA) was used as an approach for high-throughput proteomics of192 total samples. Preliminary work is expanding “MitoPaint” to stem cell-derived neuronal models, enabling investigation of mitochondrial dysfunction in systems more relevant to neurodegeneration. This novel experimental paradigm has applications in understanding mitochondrial function across broad disease biology contexts, as well as being a screening platform for identifying mitochondrial toxicity.Furthermore, the coupling of multi-modal data should offer richer insight into novel cellular mechanisms modulating mitochondrial function.

Poster number & title: 22 - Initial Insights into Cost-Efficient AI Toxicity Profiling: Cell Painting +Chemical Structures.
Abstract: Toxicity is one of the most common reasons for failure in late stagedrug development, accounting for 30% of non-successful projects.While multiple assays for various toxicity types are available, theyusually are quite costly and unfit to be run in a high-throughputsetting. This makes them only feasible at the late stage drugdiscovery, where failure results in a significant time and resourcepenalty to the project. Quantitative Structure-Activity Relationship(QSAR) toxicity prediction methods could be applied at the earlierstage of the projects, however, their use is limited to the chemicalspace of the training data and the method often fails for novelchemical structures. Here we present an endeavor to create a dataset of small moleculetreatments visualized with the target-agnostic Cell Painting assay,that captures the early onset of various types of toxicity, such ashepato-, cardio and genotoxicity. This data, screened in relevant celllines and analyzed with multimodal Artificial Intelligence algorithmsallows us to build models capable of assessing the treatment toxicitywith high accuracy and throughput. For the proof of concept project we selected a single hepatocyteHUH7 cell line and tested an initial small set of compounds withknown toxicities. The results show that using multiple modalities,here image and molecular structure, improves the predictive powerover single modality models. Additionally, we are able to detect andpredict cell-line independent toxicities, such as cardiotoxicity signalsin a hepatocyte cell line.

Poster number & title: 23 - Multiparametric assays in 3D human liver microtissues: towards multiplexed in vitro NAMs for drug-induced liver injury
Abstract: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is a significant concern for drug safety and is a key factor for post-marketing drug withdrawals. New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), such as assays utilizing InSphero’s 3D human liver microtissues,  compromised of primary liver parenchymal and non-parenchymal cells, provide a non-animal platform to assess DILI risks. Combined with viability endpoints, InSphero's 3D liver model has previously demonstrated improved sensitivity and selectivity for flagging DILI inducing compounds [Fäs et al.,2024].    To enhance mechanistic insight, we propose a multiparametric approach capturing key DILI pathways: mitochondrial dysfunction (TMRM), oxidative stress (CellROX), and bile salt export pump inhibition (Cholyl-Lysine-Fluorescein/CLF). These live-cell imaging endpoints are multiplexed with biochemical viability readouts and, in selected cases, with Organoid DRUG-Seq transcriptomics on the same microtissues. This multi-modal framework will be applied to a diverse panel of DILI-positive and DILI-negative reference compounds.  Here we present preliminary results of individual and semi-multiplexed imaging protocols using sub-lethal compound concentrations to capture early mechanistic changes. We demonstrate multiplexing of TMRM staining with the Organoid DRUG-Seq workflow. Furthermore, bile salt export pump staining with known cholestatic compounds and detection of ROS inducing compounds were successfully established.  A key challenge remains the integration of multiple assays without compromising technical or biological performance. Our findings establish a foundation for mechanistic DILI profiling that unifies functional and transcriptomic endpoints within the same 3D microtissue, aiming to extract maximal mechanistic information and ultimately improve DILI prediction.

Poster number & title: 24 - Deep Learning Frameworks for Rare Event Detection and Phenotyping in Enrichment-Free Liquid Biopsy
Abstract: Liquid biopsy provides a minimally invasive window into cancer biology, yet the rarity and heterogeneity of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) and associated events limit detection and interpretation. Traditional methods often depend on biophysical enrichment or a priori biomarker selection, introducing bias and reducing sensitivity. Scalable, unbiased computational frameworks are needed to directly analyze millions of single-cell events and extract biologically meaningful structure without prior labels. We developed deep learning frameworks to interrogate cells obtained from patient peripheral blood. Approximately five million nucleated cells per patient are isolated through buffy coat preparation, stained with a five-marker fluorescent panel, and captured by whole slide imaging without enrichment. The first framework employs a denoising autoencoder for unsupervised rare event detection. In 11 breast cancer patients, this approach identified 91 additional events—an increase of more than 50% across CTCs, endothelial cells, CAFs, and extracellular vesicles —with minimal manual optimization. This unsupervised outlier detection strategy is broadly applicable to high-content screening where unbiased identification of rare or unexpected populations is critical. The second framework leverages representation learning to generate robust single-cell embeddings. These embeddings achieve 92.64% accuracy in downstream phenotype classification and enable unsupervised clustering to reveal natural groupings based on morphology and expression. Importantly, the embeddings are resilient to imaging artifacts, supporting reliable phenotyping across diverse cohorts. Together, these frameworks provide a unified approach for rare event detection, clustering, and phenotyping in enrichment-free liquid biopsy, offering a scalable strategy for biomarker discovery.

Poster number & title: 25 - From Crystals to Collagen: SHG Microscopy Signal Generation inOrdered Protein Systems
Abstract: Second-harmonic generation (SHG) microscopy is a nonlinearoptical technique that is used to image tissues and other proteinassemblies that are noncentrosymmetric, that is, characterized bylack of an inversion center. SHG imaging provides a label-freemethod for observing a wide variety of ordered protein assemblies,including protein crystals for different structure determinationtechniques, fiber-like protein entities such as collagen and mitoticspindle microtubules, and amyloid aggregated protein plaques inneuroscience. The requirement for noncentrosymmetric materialslimits SHG to either crystalline or ‘oriented’ filamentous arrays ofproteins, such as the proteins found in linear myofibrils. Despite thisrestriction, SHG microscopy has seen wide application in imaging incrystallography, in image-based diagnostics, and in biomedicalresearch probing structural details of intact tissue. SHG relies on the generation of a frequency-doubled response inordered materials, providing an intensity measurement that informson 3D spatial organization at the molecular and optical scales. Inthis work, we are specifically exploring what features of orderedprotein systems are involved in SHG signal generation, and whethersignal intensity is predictable from molecular information and/orknowledge of the lattice/orientation information. Knowing whether aparticular protein array is capable of generating a SHG signal, and ifthe signal will be of sufficient intensity, would advance the utility andsuitability of this nonlinear optical method in all of its differentdomains of application.

Poster number & title: 26 - AI-Powered Label-Free Imaging Assay for Rapid Viral Infectivity Detection
Abstract: Infectivity assays are essential for vaccine and antiviral development, yet traditional methods like plaque and TCID₅₀ assays are slow and rely on late-stage cytopathic effects, often requiring up to 15 days to complete. Fluorescent focus assays (FFA) potentially deliver faster results, but their scalability and objectivity are limited by fluorescent labeling strategies and manual image analysis. AVIA™ (Automated Viral Infectivity Assay) is a machine learning-based platform that uses brightfield microscopy and a reliable, automated high-resolution imaging system to detect early phenotypic changes in live cells associated with viral replication. The platform enables infectivity measurements within hours, without sample prep, fluorescence, or user-defined parameters, ensuring rapid and reproducible results. AVIA is hosted on ViQi, Inc.’s cloud-based platform, which enables scalable, reproducible infectivity screening for accelerated therapeutic development. Each model is trained on a single 96-well plate with high MOI infections, controls, and dilutions, then validated across biological and technical replicates. Once trained, AVIA quantifies infection rates under experimental conditions such as antibody neutralization or viral attenuation. Here we report the detection of human rhinovirus (HRV16) infection in Vero cells as early as 16 hours postexposure using AVIA enabling rapid and precise viral titer quantification. Furthermore, two HRV16-targeting antibodies were evaluated, demonstrating viral inhibition at the 16-hour mark as quantified by AVIA. Combined, these findings highlight the capability of the platform for rapid and accurate assessment of viral infectivity through label-free image analysis.

Poster number & title: 27 - A streamlined automation solution for Cell Painting sample preparation and imaging
Abstract: Cell Painting is an established technique for image-based cell phenotyping with increasing adoption in high-throughput research programs spanning drug discovery, toxicology and functional genomics. Automation of sample preparation and imaging is critical to conduct Cell Painting assays at scale. Here we present a streamlined three-instrument solution that automates the most recent Cell Painting assay protocol from cell seeding to imaging. We provide a technical overview of bulk liquid handling instrument configuration across multiple steps of the Cell Painting protocol and validate cellular staining, distribution and retention to ensure sample consistency and reproducibility. We introduce the Agilent BioTek Cytation C10 confocal imaging reader for automated multichannel image acquisition required for the canonical Cell Painting cellular stain combination. Multichannel images were analyzed using an existing open-source CellProfiler software pipeline, demonstrating proof-of-concept compatibility with the growing ecosystem of open-source Cell Painting data analysis tools that leverage traditional and deep-learning solutions. Importantly, this automated platform supports the conventional Cell Painting protocol while remaining flexible to accommodate customized workflows using novel stain and imaging combinations, providing additional value for targeted investigations inspired by the cell painting approach.

Poster number & title: 28 - Host-Directed Antiviral Discovery Through Morphological Profiling
Abstract: The rapid evolution and emergence of new pathogenic viruses call for innovative methods to find antiviral treatments. Traditionally, antiviral drug discovery has focused on targeting viral proteins. However, host-directed therapies, which target cellular pathways exploited by viruses, offer the potential for broader-spectrum activity and reduced resistance, yet remain underexplored. Here, we present an image-based screening approach to identify host-targeted antiviral compounds against SARS-CoV-2. We adapted the Cell  Painting assay by replacing the mitochondrial stain with a virus- specific antibody and developed a high-throughput pipeline using  Cellpose and CellProfiler to extract thousands of single-cell features. Infected cells displayed distinct morphological signatures reflecting virus-induced changes, including syncytia formation and cytoskeletal alterations. We used these signatures to identify compounds that could reverse this phenotype, applying a morphology score to measure the distance to uninfected controls. Screening over 5,275 repurposable drugs, we identified multiple compounds that reversed the infected phenotype, including candidates undetected by  conventional cytopathicity and antibody-based assays. Counter- screening excluded compounds whose antiviral activity was driven  by drug-induced phospholipidosis. Pathway enrichment analysis of drug annotations revealed frequently hijacked host pathways, including those involved in innate immune responses and kinase signaling. This data-driven approach provides an unbiased view of viral replication, host-cell health, and antiviral mechanisms of action. Our approach constitutes an adaptable and scalable platform suited for diverse viral pathogens and cell systems, providing a host-centric strategy that complements traditional virus-targeted approaches.
Category: Screening Excellence: Insights from Best Case Studies

Poster number & title: 29 - A genome-wide CRISPR nuclease screen for electrophysiological phenotypes in human neurons
Abstract: A genome-wide view of the impact of genetic perturbation on the function of neurons will be a critical resource for central nervous system (CNS) drug development, enabling drug target deconvolution and the identification of novel targets for disease treatment. Quiver Bioscience is leveraging iPSC-derived neuronal cultures, CRISPR nuclease technology, high-throughput all-optical electrophysiology, and deep learning approaches to profile the consequences of gene downregulation on neuronal behavior with unprecedented scale and resolution. We have developed assay conditions for a genome-wide arrayed CRISPRn screen profiling electrophysiology in human neurons. These functional profiles include hundreds of measurements of spiking activity and action potential shape across a range of stimulus intensities and types, capturing a broad spectrum of electrophysiology relevant to pharmacology and disease. In the genome-wide screen we have measured the behavior of 17,401,349 neurons which together characterize the functional impact of over 11,000 genes. Thus far we have identified 994 genes whose depletion results in electrophysiological changes in neurons. These include SCN3A, which encodes a voltage-gated sodium channel associated with epilepsy, and ANK3, which encodes a protein involved in ion channel trafficking to the axon initial segment. TSC1 and TSC2, which dimerize to regulate mTOR signaling, have similar phenotypes in this screening context and phenocopy a stable TSC2 knockout line in this assay, validating the performance of the screen in capturing known biological relationships and recapitulating stable mutant phenotypes. When complete, the screen dataset will include ~18,000 protein-coding genes, constituting a key resource for target deconvolution and target identification.
Category: Screening Excellence: Insights from Best Case Studies

Poster number & title: 30 - Accelerating Organoid Adoption as a NAM through Standardized,Tailor-Made Assays
Abstract: The U.S. FDA and NIH are actively promoting NewApproach Methodologies (NAMs) like organoids to reduce relianceon animal models, which often fail to predict human-relevant efficacyand toxicity. However, the successful adoption of organoids requiresstandardized and reproducible technologies capable of probing thesesensitive models in their native, unperturbed state for optimal datacapture. Methods: We present a novel approach using non-toxic, live-celldyes—NucleoLIVE™ and MortaLIVE™—for viability and cytotoxicityassessment in human organoid models. These dyes were applied toheart, retinal, and brain organoids under hypoxic stress, and toendometrial organoids for preclinical toxicology screening of knowntherapeutics (e.g., Relugolix, Staurosporine, Tamoxifen). Results: Our imaging studies demonstrate that these non-toxic dyesprovide a robust and data-rich solution for viability assessment in 3Dmodels. In hypoxia studies, the dyes successfully detected elevatedcell death and stress. In endometrial organoids, the assay effectivelydistinguished between compounds with high (Staurosporine),moderate (Relugolix), and minimal (Tamoxifen) cytotoxicity. Notably,this live-cell platform was sensitive enough to identify a potentialdose-dependent, off-target toxicity from Relugolix, highlighting theassay sensitivity for detecting specific toxic thresholds. The non-toxicnature of the dyes further allowed deep staining of 3D structures,enabling optimal data capture from these valuable organoid models. Conclusion: By providing a reproducible and data-rich assay that’sideally suited for organoid cytotoxicity evaluation, NucleoLIVE™ andMortaLIVE™ non-toxic live-cell dyes are a critical enablingtechnology platform that promises to accelerate the regulatoryadoption of organoids as a NAM.

Poster number & title: 31 - Beyond the ATP Readout: A Non-Toxic, Imaging Assay to Reveal Distinct Mechanisms of Cytotoxicity
Abstract: Traditional cell viability assays, such as the CellTiter-Glo (CTG) ATPassay, are widely used in high-throughput screening for theirsimplicity. However, by providing a single, non-specific endpoint,these assays fail to distinguish between different mechanisms of cellstress or death. This limitation can obscure a compound’s truemechanism of action (MoA), leading to suboptimal drug responsedata. We present a novel, real-time image-based approach using a non-toxic nuclear dye and a non-toxic live-dead dye – NucleoLIVE™ andMortaLIVE™ - as a potential alternative to CTG. We demonstrate thepotential of our method by treating cells with reference compoundsthat induce distinct biological responses. While the CTG assaytypically shows a simple dose-dependent decrease in signal for allcompounds, our image-based assay reveals drastically differentmechanisms of cell stress and cell death Staurosporine, a pan-kinase inhibitor, caused unequivocal cell deathover time at higher doses, well-quantified by MortaLIVE’s signal. Incontrast, Thapsigargin, an ER stress inducer, and Rapamycin, anautophagy activator, caused minimal cell death at early time pointsbut induced noticeable changes in cell viability. These uniquecharacteristics, typically missed by non-specific ATP readouts, werevisible and quantifiable with NucleoLIVE and MortaLIVE. Our work highlights the potential for capturing enhanced cytotxicitydata at scale. By providing a high-throughput solution that alsocaptures a more accurate read of cellular response approach givesdrug discovery teams the efficiency of a high-throughput assay withthe crucial mechanistic data needed to make better drug discoverydecisions.

Poster number & title: 32 - Key Considerations for Live Cell Painting Screens: A Reference Guide
Abstract: Live cell painting is an emerging image-based profiling method,enabling new phenotypic measurements by studying cells in theirnative environment and by capturing kinetic data. However, itsadoption for high-throughput screens has been slow, mainly becauseof the requirement for new workflows adapted to live cells, andbecause of the lack of assays for extracting rich biological datawithout perturbing cells. Here, we report the design and deployment of a new HTS workflow,with the goal of providing a reference for drug discovery groups toimplement into their own HTS pipelines. This workflow allows tocapture new profiling data at scale and in live cells, with tools thatpreserve cell physiology. Our workflow integrates modular automation with optimizedscheduling for timing-sensitive steps, parallel assay handling, preciseenvironmental control, and a non-toxic live cell painting method thatis unique in preserving cell physiology. To evaluate performance at scale, we profiled a library ofpharmacologically active compounds using live cell painting. Theworkflow demonstrated high reproducibility, maintained consistentcell health, and delivered robust imaging performance fordownstream profiling. Morphological signatures obtained from livecell painting revealed bioactive responses across compound classes,with temporal resolution providing an added dimension for profiling. Together, these results establish automated live cell painting as ascalable approach for integration into HTS pipelines, providing apowerful bridge between discovery-scale screening and deepermechanistic biology.
Category: Screening Excellence: Insights from Best Case Studies

Poster number & title: 33 - HepG2 Genome-Wide Optical Pooled Screen Identifies Key Metabolic Pathways and Novel Gene Functions
Abstract: The recent emergence of optical pooled screening provides a powerful tool for interrogating complex biology. The rich information in imaging-based assays provides an orthogonal view into cell biology from state of the art methods such as FACS survival screens and Perturb-Seq. When done with a whole genome CRISPR library, a holistic approach to biological questions can be achieved. Here we describe a whole genome optical pooled screen in a hepatocyte-like cell model exposed to high levels of free fatty acids, glucose and insulin with a lipid droplet imaging readout and cell paint assay. We first computationally subset our phenotyping panel to just lipid droplets and demonstrate that through extensive pathway analysis we can recapitulate known metabolic pathways based on gene knock out effects. Further utilizing our high-dimensional phenotyping panel, we then explore the interplay of lipid metabolism and mitochondrial function. By doing this, we begin to discover potentially novel biological functions. This case study shows the incredible power of optical pooled screening and the new horizons that await in these rich datasets.
Category: Screening Excellence: Insights from Best Case Studies

Poster number & title: 34 - In silico drug repurposing screen with all-optical electrophysiology recordings from >10 million neurons
Abstract: CNS therapeutic development experiences higher failure rates compared to other disease areas due to inadequate data and decision-making methods. To address this challenge, Quiver Bioscience has developed a proprietary technology platform, combining human iPS cell-derived neurons, all-optical assays of electrophysiology, and machine learning data pipelines to enable high-throughput screening of neuronal function at a scale compatible with drug discovery. This functional platform can assay in a 384-well plate format the intrinsic excitability of >500,000 neurons per instrument in a single day, with single cell and single action potential resolution, to produce insights about molecules, mechanisms, targets, and disease phenotypes.  Here, we report on the application of this platform to create maps of neurophysiology by screening thousands of drugs and tool compounds in dose response. Through two test cases, comprising functional profiles for >10 million individual neurons, we demonstrate that these maps enable predictive modeling and in silico screening, unlocking a new critical data layer for CNS drug discovery. First, we assembled and screened a library of 402 tool compounds with diverse annotated classes. We built a predictive model and achieved a significant enrichment over baseline models in prediction of drug mechanism of action. Next, we assembled and screened a library of 3,000 FDA-approved drugs and development-stage compounds. We used this screening data set to conduct an in silico phenotypic screen against a human neuronal model of Tuberous Sclerosis (TSC), generating drug repurposing hypotheses which were validated in vitro and currently being tested in vivo in a mouse model of TSC.
Category: Screening Excellence: Insights from Best Case Studies

Poster number & title: 35 - Metasurface Enabled Epi-illumination Microscopy for kinetic metabolic imaging in small-volume wells
Abstract: Time-lapse high-content imaging is a promising platform for drug screening because (a) each cell’s initial state becomes its own negative control, thereby reducing the need for a large number of precious patient-derived cells; (b) drug action kinetics is revealed, (c) heterogeneity of the cell population and its response to a drug can be measured. I will briefly discuss the key challenges to developing such screens. Next, I will describe a novel imaging platform – Metasurface Enabled Epi-illumination Microscopy (MEEM) – where live cells are cultured atop of arrays of metallic nanoantennas attached to microwell bottoms [1] and imaged using a rapidly-tunable laser for mid-infrared (MIR) illumination. The vibrational contrast in the MIR band is used by us to image the proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids in the cells, obtaining images with sub-cellular resolution. With all optics below the microplate, MEEM is fully compatible with automated liquid dispensing and low-volume microwells. I will present the results of time-lapse imaging of several cell types to classify the effects of actin- and microtubule-affecting drugs on cell motility, morphology, and attachment. MEEMs ability to image heterogeneous cell populations and the advantages of kinetic vs endpoint measurements, including fewer required cells, will be highlighted [2]. I will describe how metabolic rates of cells (including de novo lipogenesis and protein synthesis) were measured at a  single-cell level using stable isotope-labelled precursors (e.g., 13C- substituted glucose) [2].  [1] Huang, S. H. et al. Lab. Chip 23, 2228–2240 (2023). [2] S. H. Huang et. al., bioRxiv 2024.09.17.613596; 2025.03.30.646207 (2025).

Poster number & title: 36 - Machine Learning Based Method for Small Molecule High Content Screening of 3D Cancer Spheroids
Abstract: Although multiparameter cellular morphological profiling (MCMP) methods and 3D biological model systems can potentially provide complex insights for pharmaceutical discovery campaigns, there have been relatively few reports combining these experimental approaches. In this study, we use the U87 glioblastoma cell line grown in a 3D spheroid format to validate a MCMP screening method. The steps of this approach include 3D spheroid treatment, cell staining, fully automated digital image acquisition, image segmentation, numerical feature extraction, and multiple machine learning (ML) approaches for cellular profiling. For comparison, we  measured the same samples after live cell microscopy with an end- point CellTiter-Glo (CTG) cell viability assay. The combined method  characterized seven reference compounds with previously reported anti-cancer/cytotoxic properties that induce quantifiably different spheroid morphologies in this assay. The method was then used to screen a library of 925 compounds that are related to kinase signaling pathways. Both unsupervised and supervised ML approaches, identified compounds that induced morphologies that are like those induced by the reference compounds. We performed a follow-up 16 point concentration-response experiment for three of these compounds selected from our profiling pipeline and confirmed their phenotype. The morphology-based concentration response for these compounds was also correlated with the CTG end-point assay. Additionally, the measured morphological phenotypes displayed different enrichment levels of commonly annotated mechanisms of action (MoAs). Our analysis was able to identify selected MoAs associated with specific phenotypic signatures. Overall, the presented screening and analysis method can distinguish between different spheroid structural changes that are caused by specific candidate anti-cancer compounds.

Poster number & title: 38 - Cell Painting and image-based profiling of patient-derived 3D organoids for drug discovery
Abstract: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) occurs in about 1 in 3,000 births. NF1 patients develop benign tumors, including cutaneous neurofibromas (cNF), plexiform neurofibromas (pNF), as well as Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors (MPNSTs). The identification of systemic treatments for NF1-associated tumors is hindered by their rarity and their high cellular heterogeneity. Current therapies for the different NF1 tumor manifestations are very limited, with only two FDA-approved treatments for one specific tumor manifestation - pNFs. pNFs are benign tumors that grow on nerves, but they can be disfiguring, cause discomfort, and can transform into malignant sarcomas. NF1 patients display varying degrees of severity and symptoms, making “one size fits all” tumor treatments not ideal. We have developed a new image analysis framework for screening therapeutic agents in NF1 patient-derived organoids of cNFs, pNFs, and MPNSTs. We present two new innovations for 3D microscopy-based image-based profiling: 1) An optimized Cell  Painting assay for organoids suspended in Matrigel, and 2) an open- source, single-cell 3D image-based profiling framework. Specifically,  our innovations include a model-free approach of 2.5D segmentation and 3D-based computer vision feature extraction. Our high-content screening approach uses 3D Cell Painting and 3D image-based profiling for personalized medicine.

Poster number & title: 39 - The Pixel: Multiplexed, live-cell imaging read-outs for disease modeling applications
Abstract: Current optical approaches are limited to capturing morphological information and protein distribution—such as cell shape, structural organization, and marker localization—but do not directly assess functional properties like barrier integrity, attachment, or adhesion. They also cannot measure electrical/contractile activity in neural and cardiac cells. Thus, functional insights are often inferred from proxy measurements or obtained through separate assays, hindering the creation of integrated, physiologically relevant datasets. CytoTronics’ Pixel electrical imaging platform addresses this gap by measuring both morphology and function from the same cultures over time. High-density electrode arrays perform field-based impedance measurements to generate “electrical images” capturing 30+ single-cell and tissue-level readouts, including attachment, motility, adhesion, and tissue barrier. Simultaneously, the same electrodes record electrophysiological signals from neural (electrical activity) and cardiac (electrical and contractile activity) cells, layering two complementary assays into an integrated measurement. We applied this approach to two disease models: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) in neurons and Cardiac Hypertrophy in cardiomyocytes. High-dimensional analyses of electrical images clearly separated disease from healthy cultures. In ALS, electrical imaging revealed altered attachment, clumping, and network organization, while neural recordings showed elevated firing rates, burst frequencies, and abnormal network dynamics. In Cardiac Hypertrophy, electrical imaging detected hallmark remodeling, including increased cell size and spreading, while contractility measurements captured slower beating and contraction kinetics. Together, these integrated morphological and activity datasets provide richer, longitudinal insight into disease mechanisms and improved detection of compound-driven phenotypic shifts than single-modality assays, supporting development of predictive, physiologically relevant in vitro disease models.

Poster number & title: 40 - Bioactive Unbiased Single-cell Compound Assessment and Ranking (Buscar)
Abstract: High-content screening (HCS) combines automated microscopy with image-based profiling to extract thousands of morphological features from individual cells, enabling large-scale, unbiased phenotypic drug screening. Despite this single-cell resolution, most current workflows aggregate cell measurements into population-level profiles (e.g., well or treatment level), discarding critical information on cell-to-cell variability, rare phenotypes, and subpopulation-specific responses. This loss of resolution can obscure off-target effects, mask toxicity mechanisms, and hinder mechanism-of-action (MOA) prediction, which are all important factors to consider when conducting phenotypic drug screens. However, current approaches to call drug hits use aggregated profiles to quantify on- and off-target signatures. Here, we introduce buscar, a computational framework that preserves and leverages single-cell image-based profiles from HCS experiments to call drug hits. By analyzing the full distribution of cell responses within each treatment condition, buscar captures heterogeneous drug effects that conventional aggregation-based pipelines overlook. Capturing the full spectrum of single-cell heterogeneity in high-content screening is essential for uncovering nuanced drug responses and advancing phenotypic drug discovery.

Poster number & title: 41 - A novel, high-content image analysis tool for assessing lysosomal morphology in cells
Abstract: Lysosomes are crucial organelles responsible for the efficient recycling of macromolecules and degradation of cellular waste. Lysosomal dysfunction is strongly associated with various diseases, including neurodegeneration, cancer, and lysosomal storage disorders. Under these pathological conditions, lysosomal morphology is often markedly altered, characterized by changes in size, shape, and subcellular distribution. To study these morphological changes at scale, we developed a novel high-content imaging (HCI) analysis pipeline designed to systematically profile lysosomal morphology across diverse cellular contexts. This tool builds on our previously published framework, MitoProfileHC (Chin et al., 2025), and leverages texture-based image features to capture and quantify lysosomal phenotypes. To validate our pipeline, we applied high-throughput applications using several disease-relevant treatment paradigms such as pharmacological perturbations and lysosome-targeting agents across various cell lines. Additionally, we generated preliminary data from super-resolution microscopy as an orthogonal approach to visualize lysosomal structures with greater spatial resolution. This serves not only as independent validation for the HCI-based morphological assay but also provides compelling proof-of-concept data demonstrating the utility of the super-resolution platform for profiling lysosomes. Altogether, our novel pipeline offers a robust and scalable solution for assessing lysosomal morphology, with broad potential to support mechanistic studies and therapeutic discovery in lysosomal biology and disease.

Poster number & title: 42 - Highly multiplexed imaging uncovers combinatorial perturbation effects of small molecule treatments
Abstract: Image-based drug profiling captures comprehensive biological effects of small molecule treatments for drug discovery applications such as small molecule target identification and mechanism of action  (MOA) prediction. However, current imaging modalities for image- based drug profiling in single cells have limited information content  for understanding molecular mechanisms of action. To address this, we conducted a 42-plex iterative indirect immunofluorescence imaging approach to profile 148 approved oncology drugs and 15 phenotypic reference compounds in human PC9 lung cancer cells. Imaged targets include readouts for cellular metabolism, DNA damage, innate immunity, signaling pathways, and (membraneless) organelles. The 42-plex panel outperformed a reduced 6-channel panel in weakly supervised single-cell drug classification (F1-scores: 0.96 vs 0.68 for single-cell image crops; 0.70 vs 0.20 for single-cell features). Feature importance analysis identified both known and novel phenotypic drug effects, confirming that the models capture biologically meaningful cellular responses. We additionally identified and genetically validated polypharmacological effects of the EGFR inhibitor osimertinib on the autophagy lysosomal pathway. These results demonstrate that increased multiplexing generates more comprehensive and MOA-specific cellular phenotypes that meaningfully encode polypharmacological effects. When combined with genetic perturbations, this approach enables systematic identification and discrimination of on-target from polypharmacological effects, providing a powerful platform for small molecule target identification.

Poster number & title: 43 - High-throughput vpCells phenotyping of global and target-specific effects of 105,000 compounds
Abstract: Morphological profiling has emerged as a powerful imaging-based approach to capture complex cellular responses to chemical and genetic perturbations. We have previously established vpCells, a high-throughput method for endogenous multicolor protein fluorescent tagging, and a clone collection of over 1,000 labeled proteins in double-tagged cell lines. In a proof-of-concept screen, we combined high-throughput microscopy, computer vision and machine learning to detect specific subcellular protein localization changes in a vpCells pool spanning 61 proteins against 1,000 compounds, successfully validating this approach for target-specific phenotyping. Here, we present an expanded platform that applies pooled vpCells screening for phenotypic annotation of a large compound library. We built a pool of 7 clones containing 14 endogenously tagged proteins alongside 8 fluorophores labeling key cellular compartments, including membranes, nuclei, nucleoli, endoplasmic reticulum, and mitochondria. This integrated system was profiled against 105,000 compounds encompassing chemical diversity libraries and approved drugs. Our analysis yielded three major findings: First, we detected 226 protein-specific compound hits, demonstrating the sensitivity of our approach for identifying target-specific effects. Second, we performed a compound-centric analysis, observing compounds with similar effects clustering together in high-dimensional phenotypic space, enabling mechanism-of-action prediction. Third, for approximately 100 compounds we observed a highly distinct vacuolization phenotype, which we characterized through detailed follow-up investigations. Our platform represents a novel hybrid high-throughput phenotypic screening approach, combining target-specific protein localization analysis with comprehensive cellular phenotyping for drug discovery applications. We also provide a companion website enabling visualization and interactive exploration of our dataset.

Poster number & title: 44 - Exploring single‐cell images and profiles together with CytoDataFrame
Abstract: Image‐based profiling involves the analysis of vast tables of profiles alongside many related cellular images. Context-switching between tables of feature data and image viewers makes it challenging to build an intuition of profiles and their corresponding cellular objects. CytoDataFrame solves this by bringing each cell or compartment object picture and feature data into one interactive table for Jupyter notebook environments. With CytoDataFrame, you can: - Keep context at a glance. Every row shows both the features (for example, size, shape, or intensity) and an image of the same cell, so you immediately know what the data represent. - Adjust on the fly. Brightness sliders and mask toggles let you explore the images directly in jupyter. For example, highlight segmentation errors or unusual cells without writing extra code. - Filter and explore. Select subpopulations such as outliers, specific phenotypes, or quality‐control failures so you can make decisions alongside the visual representation of biological objects. - Stay in your workflow. Extending Pandas DataFrames, it works with your favorite analysis and plotting commands, and exports results for downstream sharing or publication. - Integration with coSMicQC. CytoDataFrame integrates directly with coSMicQC, which is quality control software for single-cell segmentations. coSMicQC functions return CytoDataFrames so you can make quality control decisions alongside images of cells. By unifying images and profiles in a single view, CytoDataFrame accelerates troubleshooting, improves data quality checks, and helps teams spot biological patterns faster. It makes your next discovery just a click away, perfect for anyone doing high‐content imaging.

Poster number & title: 45 - Optical Pooled Screening on a flow cell: High-throughput protein and morphological profiling using the G4XTM spatial sequencer
Abstract: Optical pooled screening (OPS) is a novel approach that integrates image-based phenotyping with in-situ sequencing, enabling mapping of genetic alterations to complex phenotypes at single-cell resolution. Despite its potential, capturing multiple readouts and performing sequencing remain labor-intensive, time-consuming, and requires specialized automation equipment, thereby limiting scalability and broader adoption of OPS. The G4XTM Spatial Sequencer is a multi-omics platform that combines sequencing-by-synthesis chemistry with protein and RNA profiling within flow cells, achieving high throughput and subcellular resolution. Using this platform, we conducted two proof-of-concept OPS studies: epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in ARPE-19 cells and inflammasome response in THP1 cells. Pilot results demonstrated high sgRNA detection accuracy while effectively capturing the relevant phenotypic changes in both cell models. Next, we launched a full-scale OPS screen using an EMT-focused library to investigate the role of 703 genes in age-related macular degeneration. We successfully captured 18 protein readouts, including epithelial and EMT-focused markers. Initial QC metrics indicated excellent performance, including 99.8% library recovery, robust cell coverage (~500-750 cells/sgRNA), uniform barcode distribution, ~85% of cells detected expressing a unique gRNA sequence, and accurate cell segmentation.
