This novel integration of OPS with the G4XTM platform enabled high-fidelity protein detection and accurate genotyping, while reducing the sequencing time by 20- fold. Altogether, the G4XTM Spatial Sequencer adapted for OPS simplifies deployment, increases sequencing throughput, and supports multi-omic readouts, thus facilitating high throughput screening campaigns to uncover novel biological mechanisms.

Poster number & title: 46 - A high-throughput organoid drug screening platform combines phenotypic and stemness reporter readout
Abstract: The WNT signaling pathway is a major regulator of colorectal cancer(CRC) stemness, thereby contributing to treatment resistance, metastasis, and relapse. To identify novel drugs specifically targeting stemness, we have established a high-throughput drug screening platform combining phenotypic profiling with a targeted WNT signaling assay in CRC organoids. Using a unique collection of patient-derived organoid cultures reflecting the heterogeneous mutation, gene expression, and drug response profiles observed in the clinic, we are able to assess perturbation-induced changes across a broad range of CRC patients. In our screening approach, we are able to screen CRC organoids with hundreds of drugs per assay. To achieve reproducibility as well as scalability, we optimized critical steps in the screening procedure with a special emphasis on organoid seeding. Following treatment,3D confocal imaging of fixed and stained organoids is performed, creating millions of images and terabytes of data per screen, which are fed into our cloud-based machine learning-assisted image analysis pipeline. Upon preprocessing, segmentation, and feature extraction, a unique atlas of phenotypic profiles representing subtle phenotypic changes described by hundreds of features is created. To add an additional layer of drug-induced perturbation effects, we integrate identified phenotypes with a targeted WNT signaling reporter readout. The screening data are then linked to mutational and gene expression profiles and fed into our drug discovery knowledge base. Taken together, we here present a novel drug discovery platform to identify stemness-targeting drugs against CRC, enabled by the unique combination of high-throughput organoid screening and a machine learning-based profiling pipeline.

Poster number & title: 47 - Stellar quality control for single-cell image-based profiling with coSMicQC
Abstract: Over the past twenty years, image-based profiling has transformedour ability to measure cell phenotypes from microscopy images.However, single-cell quality control (QC) is often skipped.Conventional approaches aggregate single cells into bulk profiles,which reduces, but does not completely remove, the impact of low-quality single cells. As software improves processing scalability,single-cell image-based profiling is increasingly used to revealimportant signals of heterogeneity. Therefore, single-cell researchevolution compels single-cell QC standards to ensure that observedmorphology differences are driven by biology and not technicalinterference. We address these challenges with coSMicQC, areproducible Python package with comprehensive tutorials thatsupports systematic filtering of low-quality single cells. coSMicQCintegrates seamlessly into standard image-based profiling protocols,providing an interactive, Jupyter-compatible user interface to detecttechnical outliers. We applied coSMicQC to multiple real-worlddatasets, showing an improvement in data quality and machinelearning model performance. When applied to a large-scale drugscreening dataset, coSMicQC also changed the ranks of leadcompounds. Overall, coSMicQC is a reliable and understandablemethod that maximizes removal of technical outliers to reduce noiseand improve image-based profiling insights.

Poster number & title: 49 - Fluorescence Channel Elimination Analysis in Multiparametric Morphological Profiling of 3D Spheroids
Abstract: In this study, we used the U87 glioblastoma cell line grown in a 3Dspheroid format to validate a multiparameter cellular morphologicalprofiling (MCMP) screening method, with a focus on optimizingfluorescence channels. The workflow included spheroid treatment,cell staining, fully automated image acquisition, segmentation,numerical feature extraction, and application of multiple machinelearning approaches for phenotypic profiling. Our methodsuccessfully characterized the phenotypic effects of 7 referencecompounds with known anticancer activity, each inducing distinctand quantifiable spheroid morphologies. We then screened a kinase-focused small molecule library of 925 compounds, uncoveringdiverse morphological phenotypes. A key feature of this study is thestrategic elimination and optimization of fluorescence channels usedfor profiling. By testing different channel combinations, we explore ifhigh-quality morphological information can be retained whilereducing the number of fluorescent markers—potentially loweringassay cost, minimizing phototoxicity, and increasing throughput. Thisstreamlined approach is particularly advantageous for 3D models,where imaging challenges and signal degradation complicatetraditional fluorescence-based workflows. Our findings suggest thatselective channel elimination can preserve analytical depth withoutcompromising biological insight depending on the fluorescentchannels being used. Ultimately, this refined 3D MCMP pipelineenhances the utility of phenotypic screening in more physiologicallyrelevant cancer models, paving the way for broader adoption in high-throughput drug discovery.

Poster number & title: 50 - Live cell painting of an induced microglia model uncovers dynamic cellular phenotypes
Abstract: Microglia, the resident immune cells of the brain, have beenimplicated in the pathology of several neurodegenerative diseases.However, their location in the brain has also made it difficult to 1)isolate and culture large numbers of microglia, and 2) study how theychange in real time as they encounter disease-associated stressorsand stimuli. To solve the challenge of microglia isolation and culture,we used an inducible microglia model that can be grown at scale. Inorder to study in an unbiased manner how microglia respond tostress, we implemented a live cell painting workflow and analysispipeline to capture both human interpretable and representationbased phenotypes. We captured dynamic phenotypes includingchanges in cellular movement and increases in lipid dropletformation associated with IFNb treatment. Our work enables livecharacterization of microglia response to stress and lays thegroundwork for future studies for this dynamic cell type.

Poster number & title: 51 - Viral Infectivity from Brightfield Images using Deep Learning Models
Abstract: Current methods of in vitro screening for efficacious viral inhibitorcompounds or vaccines typically requires engineering of a tool virusto incorporate a fluorescent reporter protein, or developing an assaythat specifically measures virus-associated proteins or nucleic acids,as well as performing a separate measurement to differentiatebetween compound efficacy and toxicity. High-throughput, label-free,brightfield (BF) imaging of cells in vitro using a traditional high-content screening microscope, combined with advanced deeplearning models, can enable the detection of subtle cell phenotypesthat differentiates between healthy and infected cells. Thistechnology has the potential to identify the infection phenotype ofvarious native virus strains and provide an earlier, faster, and simplerreadout of viral inhibition. Our EfficientNetB0 based deep learning(DL) model trained solely on BF images from RSV-A infected HEp-2cells achieved greater than 99% accuracy in detecting the infectedvs. non-infected wells of assay plates. The trained model is accurate,generalizable, and capable of capturing virus titration curves acrossassays without retraining. We applied the BF DL model to themeasurement of RSV-A infected HEp-2 cells dosed with viral inhibitorcompounds and compared results to the standard reporter-basedinfection readout. The deep learning analysis method demonstratedstrong agreement with the reporter-based readout, while alsoproviding additional data on compound toxicity in the samemeasurement. This BF-DL measurement and analysis technology ishighly automatable and shows strong promise in enabling moreefficient compound screening.

Poster number & title: 52 - ML-Assisted High-Content Imaging for Keratinocyte Differentiation:Case Study with Nymphaea alba
Abstract: Keratinocyte differentiation is central to epidermal barrier function,and its dysregulation underlies skin barrier defects and inflammatorydisease. Conventional monitoring via KRT1 intensity fails to capturethe morphological and functional features of cornification. We developed a machine learning-assisted high-content imaging(HCI) workflow, compatible with high-content screening, to provide acomprehensive and scalable readout of keratinocyte differentiation.Immortalized hTERT keratinocytes were induced to differentiateunder calcium stimulation, with or without pretreatment with 4-phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA), and treated with Nymphaea alba FlowerExtract (NFE), a botanical with reported anti-glycation activity.Automated imaging and segmentation of KRT1-immunostained cellswith nuclear counterstain yielded multiparametric single-cell features(5,000 cells/condition). A supervised classifier integrated thesefeatures to assign differentiation states. The workflow demonstrated high reproducibility and sensitivity,confirming calcium-induced differentiation and resolving 4-PBAmodulated phenotypes. Importantly, it detected NFE-associateddifferentiation changes that were missed by intensity-only analysis.This collaborative case study with NFE demonstrates how theworkflow can support systematic evaluation of industry-relevantbioactives in the context of epidermal barrier research. In summary, this machine learning-assisted HCI platform enablesrobust, multiparametric quantification of keratinocyte differentiationbeyond conventional marker-based readouts. More broadly, itsupports high-throughput screening and discovery of modulators ofepithelial differentiation.

Poster number & title: 53 - Targeting Actin Polymerization in Myeloid Cells to Enhance Clearance of Large Amyloid Beta Aggregate
Abstract: Alzheimer’s disease is a neurodegenerative disorder that is characterized by large extracellular deposits of amyloid beta (Aβ) plaques in the brain. Microglia, the primary immune cells in the brain, interact with Aβ plaques, but their roles in plaque clearance remain poorly understood. A recent study shows that microglia use a mechanism called digestive exophagy to clear amyloids. In this process, microglia polymerize cortical actin to create an extracellular compartment that encapsulates Aβ, which is then degraded by secreted lysosomal enzymes. From these findings, we aim to develop a high-throughput screening (HTS) strategy using confocal microscopy to identify compounds that modulate digestive exophagy. Additionally, we are using sophisticated imaging processing techniques to analyze the effects of these drugs on various cellular features to better understand how those contribute toward plaque clearance. From these findings, we will generate new understandings of microglial clearance of amyloids that are potentially translatable into novel strategy of therapeutic intervention in Alzheimer’s disease.

Poster number & title: 54 - A novel gas-permeable platform provides superior optical properties and enhanced physiological relevance
Abstract: We have recently completed several rounds of evaluation using the new gas-permeable cell culture plates (InnoCellTM, manufactured by Mitsui Chemicals Inc.) for high-content imaging across multiple biological models, including HepG2 liver cancer cells, intestinal and liver organoids, and pulmonary fibrosis cell models.  The InnoCellTM plates demonstrate several key advantages that make them a promising platform for high-throughput screening. Their superior optical properties are particularly noteworthy, with Hoechst staining showing ~10-fold enhancement in signal-to-background ratio compared to transwell inserts, which is attributed to the InnoCellTM plates' significantly lower autofluorescence. The plates also successfully supported pharmacologic dose-response assays on HepG2 cells, yielding IC₅₀ values consistent with widely adopted Revvity plates.  The gas-permeable nature of the plates supports the formation of more complex cellular structures which could prove valuable for advanced disease modeling. Importantly, InnoCellTM plates allow us to culture highly functional human epithelial alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells in vitro, differentiate AT2 cells into AT1 cells that recapitulate key morphological and molecular differences observed between AT2 to AT1 cell fate transitions in a high-throughput format, and perform high-content imaging and deep phenotyping to interrogate the molecular mechanisms driving healthy or pathological differentiation of AT2 to AT1 transitions in pulmonary fibrosis.  In conclusion, the InnoCellTM plates offer significant technical improvements over conventional plates, particularly in imaging performance and the maintenance of physiologically relevant cellular structures. These advantages position the InnoCellTM plates as a superior alternative for demanding research applications, including drug screening and mechanistic studies that require high-quality imaging and optimal gas exchange.

Poster number & title: 55 - Spatially-Resolved Epithelial Barrier Function Prediction in Patient Derived Intestinal Organoids
Abstract: Intestinal organoid monolayers provide a platform to study tight junction dynamics and epithelial barrier integrity in inflammatory bowel diseases. Enteroids were established from LGR5+ intestinal stem cells isolated from ulcerative colitis patient biopsies. Traditionally, barrier function is assessed on transwell plates using transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and tracer flux assays. However, these approaches are low-throughput, failure proneoisy, lack mechanistic resolution, and are poorly suited for imaging. High-content imaging offers an opportunity to leverage morphological data for insight into epithelial responses to inflammation and injury. Here, we integrate machine vision with paired real-time TEER measurements to predict TEER outcomes and identify regions contributing to barrier integrity changes. We exposed enteroid monolayers to TNFα/IFNγ, monitored continuous TEER, then fixed/stained, and imaged the samples. A MaxViT-based machine vision model was trained on RGB images with Hoechst, Claudin-2 and ZO-1, to predict TEER. The MaxViT model outperformed XGBoost models, achieving an R² of 0.94, indicating excellent TEER prediction from images alone. We then successfully transitioned monolayers to Mitsui InnoCell gas-permeable plates that are superior for imaging and provide a supportive environment for enteroid monolayers. This enables high-throughput and regional TEER prediction in imaging plates. Upon TNFα/IFNγ stimulation, we observed changes in TEER, and MaxViT attention maps revealed neighborhoods of cellular reorganization and ZO-1 disruption, establishing that barrier function loss is focal rather than homogeneous despite uniform pro-inflammatory stimulation. This technique enables HCS while delivering spatially-resolved functional TEER prediction, facilitating mechanistic inquiry into epithelial barrier integrity regulation in patient-derived enteroids.

Poster number & title: 56 - Automated Ultra-Fast HCI Enables High Throughput Live Cell Assays with Submicron Resolution
Abstract: Live-cell imaging provides insights into cellular behaviors often missed by traditional fixed-endpoint methods: capturing transient and dynamic processes across hours or days without the distortion or artifacts of fixation. Robust effects may be overlooked because cells were fixed too early or late. Throughput in live-cell high-content imaging has been limited by acquisition speed and instrument availability. If it takes an hour or two to image a plate, then is the first well imaged in the same state as the last? Speed constraints further limit the number of timepoints and plates acquired. This poster demonstrates how to overcome this challenge with the Araceli Endeavor’s uncompromising imaging speed: ~1,000 cells/well can be imaged in less than 30 seconds and just over 1 minute for entire 96 and 384wp, respectively, with submicron resolution in 5 channels. This speed has another important consequence for live cell imaging: maintaining cell health by minimizing time out of an incubator. Using machine learning-based phenotyping, we demonstrate that these shorter imaging times preserve cellular morphology compared to traditional workflows.  Paired with automation, we demonstrate that the Endeavor Pro platform can image >476 million cells in 24 hours, at full resolution with <0.1% of images out of focus. 165 1536-well plates were imaged in a single day, making it feasible to image ~14 plates every 2 hours without sacrificing assay quality. This capability unlocks a new class of high-content, time-resolved assays that reveal subtle and transient phenotypes at scale, accelerating drug discovery, functional genomics, and cell biology research

Poster number & title: 57 - Massively paralleled genome-wide, optical pooled screen of TMED receptor abundance and localization
Abstract: The toxic accumulation of misfolded or mislocalized mutant proteins precipitates the development of several forms of tubular kidney disease (i.e. ADTKD-MUC1). Previous work from our lab has identified the involvement of the transmembrane emp24 domain (TMED) family of protein cargo receptors in this disease process. However, the exact roles and functions of TMEDs in regulating protein cargo trafficking within the secretory pathway remain poorly understood. Although the expression and subcellular localization of the TMEDs are crucial for their function, it is unknown what regulates these aspects of TMED biology. We therefore performed a genome-wide optical pooled screen of TMED abundance and localization within the secretory pathway in tubular kidney epithelial cells. We found that TMED expression was ablated by the corresponding gTMED and unaffected in both non-targeting and intergenic controls. Moreover, we identified several novel genetic regulators of TMED abundance and secretory localization. Future research will mechanistically interrogate the role of these regulators in the control of TMED function.

Poster number & title: 58 - VISTA Consortium launch: Optical Pooled Screening for Efficient Drug Testing
Abstract:
The Broad Institute is organizing a new pharma Consortium, VISTA:Variant Integration for Screening Therapeutic Approaches. Together with industry partners, we will pilot a parallel experimental and computational screening platform to identify candidate drugs for each of 250 disease-causing gene variants that cause 100 different genetically-defined disorders. VISTA combines two key recent advances from the collaborating team’s labs: the discovery of protein mislocalizations for hundreds of diseases, and massively parallel drug testing using optical pooled screens (OPS). Pooling is transformative: allowing us to move beyond the current inefficient one-by-one approach. Partners will have a front row seat observing the application of OPS which could guide internal implementation and testing of shelved and late-stage compounds for repositioning.The experiment will uncover clusters of diseases with similar mechanisms that might aggregate patient populations to a market size suited for commercial development.
Success in VISTA would not only provide treatments for several diseases, but also validate a powerful new paradigm for drug discovery, propelling forward multiple fields including functional genomics, image analysis, and machine learning for biology - all of which can then accelerate drug discovery.
VISTA is in the organizing stage and open to new members! Join thec ollaborating teams at the Broad Institute of Harvard and MIT and the University of Toronto in this project: Anne Carpenter-Shantanu Singh, JT Neal, Mikko Taipale, Beth Cimini, Paul Blainey, and more.

Poster number & title: 59 - Integrated DRUG-seq and Cell Painting Profiling of JUMP MoA Compounds in U2OS and HepG2 Cell
Abstract:
Comprehensive mechanism of action (MoA) characterization benefits from combining orthogonal phenotypic and transcriptomic profiling technologies. In this study, we compared DRUG-seq, a high-throughput RNA-sequencing–based transcriptomic assay, with Cell Painting, a high-content morphological imaging approach, using the JUMP-MoA compound set across two cell lines, U2OS and HepG2. Identical compound treatments were profiled using both methods to evaluate clustering performance, reproducibility, and the complementarity of biological information captured. 
DRUG-seq produced a higher number of differentially expressed genes and stronger inter-replicate correlations, supporting its robustness and sensitivity for capturing compound-induced transcriptional changes. Cell Painting provided complementary insights into morphological phenotypes and displayed more consistent cross-cell-type clustering, highlighting its strength in capturing generalizable phenotypic features. Integrating DRUG-seq and Cell Painting data improved MoA inference, enabling richer cross-platform validation and a more comprehensive understanding of compound activity. 
Together, these results emphasize the value of combining transcriptomic and morphological profiling approaches to generate multi-dimensional biological fingerprints that enhance discovery and interpretation in drug screening and mechanistic studies.
